summary: Defines a YANG module for managing the reverse metric extension to the IS-IS routing protocol. The module lets operators configure and view this feature through standard network management tools.

eli5.summary: A standard settings page for a feature that lets routers ask neighbors to adjust traffic sent their way.

what is the is-is reverse metric yang module
what does enable-receive do in is-is
what is the whole lan bit in is-is reverse metric
subtitle: A standard YANG data model for configuring and inspecting the IS-IS reverse metric feature on routers.

tldr.problem: RFC 8500 defines a way for an IS-IS router to ask its neighbors to adjust the metric they use for a link, but there was no standard data model for configuring or viewing that feature.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the ietf-isis-reverse-metric YANG module, which adds reverse metric settings to the IS-IS data model: a global switch for receiving, per-interface values to announce, and read-only data about what neighbors announced.
tldr.outcome: Operators and management systems can use NETCONF or RESTCONF to manage reverse metric in a uniform way. The module is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9194 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the YANG data model for the reverse metric functionality of RFC 8500.

sections.title: What This Module Manages
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG module for managing the reverse metric extension to IS-IS. The functionality itself is described and defined in RFC 8500, so this RFC adds no new protocol behavior. It only supplies a data model for configuring and viewing it.

The model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture defined in RFC 8342.
sections.eli5: The feature already exists. This document only describes the settings page for it, like a remote control for a gadget someone else invented.

sections.title: The YANG Tree
sections.content:
The module, named ietf-isis-reverse-metric, makes three augmentations to the routing model from RFC 8349 and the IS-IS model from RFC 9130.

  • On the IS-IS instance, a reverse-metric container with one leaf, enable-receive.
  • On each IS-IS interface, a read-write reverse-metric container with a metric, flags and exclude-te-metric, plus separate level-1 and level-2 copies of the same settings.
  • On each adjacency, a read-only reverse-metric container showing what the neighbor announced.
sections.eli5: There are three groups of controls: one switch for the whole router, a set of dials for each link, and a read-only display showing what each neighbor asked for.

sections.title: Receiving and Announcing Settings
sections.content:
Handling of reverse metric from neighbors is off by default. The leaf enable-receive defaults to false and must be explicitly enabled through configuration.

On an interface, announcing is enabled by configuring a metric value either at the top level of the container or under a level-specific container. If it is only set under a level-specific container, operation is enabled only at that level. Because the reverse metric is advertised in IS-IS Hello PDUs (IIH PDUs), the level-1 and level-2 containers are available only for broadcast interface types. The structure follows the same per-level hierarchical behavior as the augmented base module.
sections.eli5: By default a router ignores such requests until you flip a switch. When you want to make a request yourself, you set a number on a link, and for some kinds of links you can set different numbers for the two levels of the network.

sections.title: The Flags and the TE Metric
sections.content:
Each interface has two flags, taken from RFC 8500, both defaulting to false.

  • whole-lan (the W bit): if true, a Designated Intermediate System (DIS) that processes the reverse metric adds the value to all the nodes it advertises in the pseudonode LSP for the interface. Otherwise it only increments the metric for the advertising node.
  • allow-unreachable (the U bit): if true, the neighbor may raise the overall metric up to 2^24-1 instead of the lesser maximum of 2^24-2. Setting it to 2^24-1 makes traffic stop using the interface rather than merely avoid it.

The exclude-te-metric leaf (default false) suppresses the Traffic Engineering Metric sub-TLV in the Reverse Metric TLV when a TE metric is defined. On the read-only adjacency side, a te-metric leaf of type uint32 shows the TE metric from the sub-TLV, if present.
sections.eli5: One flag says whether the request applies to everyone on a shared link or just one router. The other says whether a neighbor may make the link so costly that nobody uses it at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users may reach which data.

The writable nodes can enable, disable and change the metrics used by routing, so unprotected writes can harm network operations. The RFC lists them: enable-receive, and on each interface the metric, both flags and exclude-te-metric, at the top level and under level-1 and level-2. The readable adjacency nodes may also be sensitive. For the implications of the feature itself, the RFC points to RFC 8500 and RFC 9130.
sections.eli5: Changing these dials can steer traffic around a whole network, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch them, over a secure connection.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The appendix gives three examples of YANG instance data. The first, in XML, sets enable-receive to true for an IS-IS instance. The second, in XML, configures a metric of 65535 on interface eth0. The third, in JSON, sets a Level-1-only reverse metric of 65535 on eth0 together with exclude-te-metric set to true.
sections.eli5: The examples are filled-in forms showing how to turn the feature on and how to set a number on one link.
